short: Eight thousand life-size clay soldiers buried to guard China's first emperor.
full:
Work on Qin Shi Huang's mausoleum below Mount Li began in 246 BCE, the year he took the Qin throne as a boy of thirteen, and ran for close to four decades on conscripted labour. A mile and a half east of the burial mound, in three pits, his builders drew up an army in battle order: more than 8,000 infantry, 130 chariots and some 670 horses, all at life size. Heads, torsos and limbs were moulded separately and luted together, then finished by hand, so that no two faces repeat. Over 40,000 bronze weapons have been recovered from the pits, many of them still sharp.

The figures were sealed around 210 to 209 BCE, painted in bright mineral pigments that flake within minutes of exposure to air, and the pits were burned and looted soon after the dynasty fell. Farmers digging a well at Lintong struck a terracotta head on 29 March 1974. Most of the complex, including the tomb mound that Sima Qian described as holding rivers of mercury, is still unexcavated; soil surveys have found mercury concentrations consistent with his account.
